paragraphs.source_en: When I explained the exercise called “going round the bamboo fence,” I believe I briefly mentioned that my master's garden was enclosed by a bamboo fence. But please do not misunderstand and suppose that immediately outside this bamboo fence there is a neighbor's house. That is to say, do not imagine that someone of the sort called a dear little so-and-so is his neighbor. Cheap though the rent may be, Kushami is still Kushami; he would never make neighbors of the sort who go by such pet names, carrying on intimate relations with them across a single garden fence. Outside this bamboo fence lies an open space of three or four jō, and at the far end stand five or six luxuriant cypresses in a row. Seen from my master's veranda, the opposite side looks like a dense grove, giving the impression that the master is a recluse of the world, passing his days with a nameless cat as his companion. However, the branches of those cypresses are not as thick as advertised, so through them one can plainly see the roof of a lodging house called the “Hall of Gathered Cranes,” a name of great elegance for what is in fact no more than a third- or fourth-rate boarding house. Naturally, it is rather difficult to imagine just what sort of fellows might be living in that lodging house. If that small lodging house may be called the Hall of Gathered Cranes, then Mr. Kushami's honorable residence is surely worthy of being called the Reclining Dragon's Cave. After all, there is no tax on names, so both sides may freely give themselves grand and formidable ones. This open space, four or five jō wide, runs along the bamboo fence east and west for seven or eight jō or so, then suddenly bends at a right angle and encloses the Reclining Dragon's Cave on the north. It is precisely this northern side that became the source of the disturbance. On the north, originally, open space continued into more open space, surrounding two sides of the house where my master lived. But not only the master of the Reclining Dragon's Cave; even I have been sorely troubled by this vacant ground. Just as the south side has cypresses that make quite a show of things, the north side has seven or eight paulownia trees standing in a row. The trunks of these paulownias have already reached about a foot in diameter, and if one brought in the owner of a clog shop, they would fetch a good price. Sadly, however, my master is only a tenant in a rented house; though he knows the trees have value, he can do nothing about it. I can only feel the deepest sympathy for my master. The other day, a school janitor came and cut off one branch; when he came the second time, he was wearing a pair of paulownia clogs and, though no one had asked him, boasted, “These were made from that branch I cut off.” A truly sly fellow he is. There are paulownia trees, to be sure, but for me and for my master's family they are paulownias that will not yield a single coin. There is an old saying, I am told, that one who holds jade is guilty; in our case one might say we keep paulownias and have no money, a case of letting treasure rot in one's hands. The fool who does this is neither my master nor I, but the landlord, Denbei. The paulownias seem to be urging, “Isn't anyone coming to cut us down? Isn't anyone coming to cut us down?” But the landlord pays no attention to any of this and only comes to collect the rent. I bear no old grudge against Denbei, so I shall stop speaking ill of him here.

paragraphs.source_zh: 在我说明“绕竹墙”这个运动的时候，我记得曾经提起过主人家的院子是用竹篱笆围起来的。但是请不要误会，以为在这个竹篱笆外立刻就有邻居。也就是说，不要以为有什么叫做哥儿们的人是他的邻居。别看房租很贱，苦沙弥毕竟是苦沙弥，他是不会和号称哥儿们的那类人结成邻居，同他们只隔着一道院墙亲密往来的。这个竹墙外边有三四丈的空地，空地的尽头排列着五六株郁郁苍苍的扁柏。从主人家的廊子望出去，对面是茂密的树林，给人一种主人乃是以无名的猫儿为友、消磨岁月的江湖之士的感觉。不过，这扁柏的枝头并不像所吹嘘的那样茂密，所以从其间可以清晰地看到一家名叫“群鹤馆”的公寓屋顶，尽管这个公寓名称高雅得很，其实只不过是个三四流的公寓罢了。当然，去想象住在那座公寓里的老兄们都是些什么人，是相当不容易的。如果这个小公寓可以称为群鹤馆，那么苦沙弥先生的尊居称为卧龙窟也就当之无愧了。反正叫什么名字是毋需纳税的，所以彼此尽可以取一个吓人的名字。这块宽度有四五丈的空地顺着竹篱，东西延伸七八丈左右，立刻直角拐过去，从北面围住卧龙窟。就是这个北面成了闹事儿的根源。北面原本是空地接着空地，包围着我家主人住的房子的两面。但是卧龙窟的主人自不必说，就连我也为这片空地而大伤脑筋。南面由于长着扁柏显得很像回事一样，北面并排长着七八株梧桐树。这些桐树的树干直径已有一尺左右，如果把木屐铺的老板领来，是会卖到好价钱的。但可悲的是主人是租房的房客，尽管他了解这树值钱，毕竟无法付之行动。我只能对主人深表同情。前些天，学校的工友来，砍走了一根树枝，他第二次来的时候，穿了一双桐木做的木屐，并无人问他，他却自我吹嘘说：“这就是用砍走的树枝做的。”这家伙真够得上狡猾啦。即使有桐树，不过对我、对主人一家，是连一文钱的好处也得不到的。古语中曾有句话叫做“怀玉有罪”，我们这里也可以说是穷守着桐树而一文不名，也就是所谓“抱着金碗要饭”。干这种傻事的，不是我家主人，也不是我，而是房东传兵卫。桐树似乎在催促：“怎么还不来砍呀？怎么还不来砍呀？”但房东却根本不理会这些，只知道收房租。我和传兵卫并无宿怨，关于他的坏话，我就说到此为止。
